title: Bohlale Katsaros

body:
Bohlale offers healing, watches Minerva’s place while she is away and welcomes the work of people who keep a settlement going. His jokes and stories about an old fighting company accompany a willingness to help here.

Meeting the people who keep the town going

At the Honest Shops, Bohlale recognizes Pell and sees new faces with Camilla. Pell introduces him as the person who brought him through the Gate. Bohlale introduces himself as a keeper of peace and makes time to ask who the newcomers are. He mistakes Zelaria’s relation to Blud, and their correction stays part of the exchange.

His shield bears a divine symbol unfamiliar to these lands. The scene does not identify that god or make his faith the faith of Prima. He remembers his lost wife through a joke about her temper, and later remembers a crew who were wild in battle and relaxed afterward. Those are glimpses he gives of a life whose broader history is not supplied here.

Offers with work still attached

He asks Camilla about her former group. She tells him it has been folded into the Pristinian militia and describes the difficulty of training people who are still bakers, smiths and farmers. Bohlale answers as someone who says he has led a company himself. He offers assistance and tells her where to find him.

He says he mostly stays at Minerva’s place in Eovar and watches it while she is away. Her later return puts that responsibility in an ordinary setting: a place kept running for someone who has been elsewhere. He quietly gives Pell gold and speaks of another overnight watch. These actions do not establish a new official office or a completed militia reform.

He hopes to help as a scout once he has a license. The qualification matters: saying he will do it is not the same as already holding it.

A healer with old fights in his stories

Bohlale calls himself more a healer than a fighter, while insisting he knows his way around a battle. He tells the others about resistance fighters in his homeland and a lich defeated repeatedly, including by his own hand. That extraordinary history remains his story; this scene does not independently establish its battles.

His worries here are more immediate. He asks about the hags, admits that most arcane practice lies outside his understanding, and seeks a devotional amulet. He offers his service to the people before leaving. His history in Prima is still emerging, with the watch, welcome and practical help clearer than the achievements he recounts from home.

A conversation at the harbor

At Eovar Harbor, Bohlale again identifies himself with watching Minerva’s place. Clive asks about changes in the harbor and the refugees’ need for homes. Their frustration turns to materials. Bohlale says supplies are going to Gael and attributes the decision to Minerva, while admitting he has not yet asked her why.

That exchange is a complaint and a plan to seek an explanation, not an audited account of every shipment. Bohlale says he still lacks the license that would let him gather. His offer of service therefore has practical limits alongside it.
